endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Device Software Functions: Lifecycle Management and Marketing Submission Recommendations (draft guidance)
endorsements.quote: If patient and 663 caregiver-specific material is not provided, sponsors should provide an explanation of how 664 patients and caregivers will understand how to use the device, including how to make decisions 665 about whether to use the device and how to use the output of the device.

endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: Also determine whether end users and patients will receive the same documentation (given various levels of expertise and health literacy).

commentary.bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether separate patient- and caregiver-facing labeling for AI tools improves understanding, safe use, or decisions, and no study documents the hazard directly. The recommendation currently rests on an FDA draft guidance and the CHAI Assurance Standards Guide, both of which use 'should' language.

perspectives.view: No studies test the practice and no studies document the hazard, so the certainty rating is no direct evidence. The two endorsements reflect expert and regulatory judgment rather than measured outcomes. A claim that tailored labeling improves comprehension or safe use of AI tools would require comparative testing against clinician-oriented documentation.

The FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software functions asks sponsors either to provide patient- and caregiver-specific material or to explain how patients will understand device use and output. The document is a draft and does not bind sponsors. The CHAI guide asks deployers to decide whether patients and clinicians receive the same documentation.

The CHAI guide names health literacy as a reason to consider separate materials, while the FDA draft text supplied here does not mention it. No supplied study measures comprehension among low-literacy, limited English proficiency, Medicaid, or safety-net patients, so health systems lack evidence on which formats, reading levels, or languages would serve these groups.

commentary.research_gap: Studies should compare patient-tailored AI labeling with clinician-oriented documentation, measuring comprehension, correct use of device output, and decision quality, and should report how often patients currently receive documentation they cannot understand.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice in any population, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. The health-literacy rationale stated in the CHAI guide remains untested in the groups it is meant to protect.
